title: Most consistent scorers (rate of 30+ scores with 95% CI)
finding: RD Gaikwad reaches 30 in 55.4% of 65 innings (95% CI 43.3-66.8%). The intervals are wide: 10 of the top 10 have a lower bound at or below the 10th-ranked player's rate (45.5%), so the order within the top 10 is not statistically settled. However, 10 of the top 10 have a lower bound above the median qualifying batter's rate (31.5%), so they are reliably more consistent than a typical batter.

title: Frequency of 30+, 50+ and 100+ scores
sample: League: 16,842 batting innings. Ranking: batters with >= 50 innings (n = 103).
finding: League-wide, 24.4% of innings reach 30, 10.6% reach 50 and 0.60% reach 100. DA Warner reaches 50 most often (35.9% of innings). Among batters with 20+ scores of 50 or more, JC Buttler converts best (7 hundreds from 26 innings of 50+, 26.9%).

title: Scoring distribution
sample: 12 leading run scorers (2,366 innings); skewness for all 103 batters with >= 50 innings.
finding: Every qualifying batter's score distribution is right-skewed (skewness > 0 for 103 of 103); the median innings is below the mean for all 12 leaders (12/12). Example: V Kohli's median innings is 25 vs a mean of 32.8. Averages therefore overstate a 'typical' innings; medians and milestone rates (A1-A2) describe reliability better.

title: Boundary % and dot-ball %
finding: SP Narine hits a boundary off 28.2% of balls. Across batters, the relationship between boundary % and dot % is weak and not statistically significant (rho = 0.13, p = 0.137) - both styles (boundary-heavy with many dots, and low-dot rotation) exist side by side. Strike rate tracks boundary % (rho = 0.84) more closely than low dot % (rho = -0.32).

title: Death-overs acceleration
sample: Batters with >= 250 death balls and >= 500 balls in overs 1-15 (n = 51).
finding: League-wide, strike rate rises by 32.6 in the death overs. AB de Villiers accelerates most (+94.5: 128.4 -> 222.9), followed by DJ Bravo (+78.7). 51 of 51 qualifying batters score faster at the death; the smallest change is N Pooran (+11.9).

title: Season-to-season variability
sample: Seasons with >= 100 balls faced; batters with >= 6 such seasons (n = 62).
finding: The steadiest batter is JP Duminy (season-adjusted strike rate varies by SD 5.4 over 7 seasons); the most variable is HH Pandya (SD 27.5, from 113 to 191). The median SD across qualifying batters is 15.1 strike-rate points. Much of this is sampling noise: with a per-ball run SD of 1.65, a season's strike rate has a standard error of about 16 points at 100 balls and 10 at 250 balls.

title: Batting first vs chasing
sample: Batters with >= 30 innings in both roles (n = 74).
finding: Median strike rate is 133.6 batting first vs 131.8 chasing (Wilcoxon p = 0.320); median runs per innings 23.0 vs 23.5 (p = 0.115). Chasing innings are cut short when the target is reached (median not-out rate 20% chasing vs 11% batting first), so lower runs per innings when chasing is expected and is NOT evidence of weaker batting. Individual differences (e.g. DR Smith +24.8) are not tested one by one to avoid multiple-comparison false positives.

title: Wicket-taking rate and dismissal mix by phase
finding: A bowler wicket falls every 13.5 balls at the death vs 26.7 in the Powerplay and 24.9 in the middle overs. The dismissal mix differs by phase (chi-square = 160, dof = 10, p = 3.9e-29): caught is 71% of death wickets vs 68% in the Powerplay; stumpings are 4.8% of middle-overs wickets vs 1.5% (Powerplay) and 2.1% (death), and bowled/lbw shares are highest in the Powerplay (28%). Bowler type is not in the data, so the link to spin in the middle overs is a plausible explanation, not a finding.

title: Economy vs wicket-taking trade-off (season- and phase-adjusted)
finding: Phase/season adjustment changes the picture: SP Narine is the most economical relative to context (-1.57 runs/over). Across bowlers, the rank correlation between adjusted economy and strike rate is rho = -0.11 (p = 0.335) - no statistically significant trade-off: being economical neither costs nor guarantees wickets. 23 of 76 bowlers beat the league on BOTH measures (e.g. Rashid Khan, JJ Bumrah, SL Malinga, CV Varun, Harbhajan Singh).

title: Dot-ball and boundary-conceding percentages
finding: DW Steyn has the highest dot-ball rate (46.8%); M Muralitharan concedes the fewest boundaries (11.2% of balls). Boundary % explains economy more strongly (rho = 0.87) than dot % (rho = -0.11): limiting boundaries matters more for run control than bowling dots. Note: dot % and boundary % are not era-adjusted (both shift with scoring levels).

title: Death-overs specialists (season-adjusted)
sample: Bowlers with >= 600 legal balls in the death (n = 18).
finding: SP Narine is the standout death bowler (-2.36 runs/over vs league; raw economy 7.40, strike rate 14.0), then JJ Bumrah (-1.65) and SL Malinga (-1.61). 10 of 18 qualifying bowlers beat the league rate.

title: Powerplay specialists (season-adjusted)
sample: Bowlers with >= 600 legal balls in the powerplay (n = 36).
finding: B Kumar is the standout powerplay bowler (-1.45 runs/over vs league; raw economy 6.39, strike rate 29.9), then JJ Bumrah (-1.35) and SL Malinga (-1.12). 26 of 36 qualifying bowlers beat the league rate.

title: Bowlers consistent across seasons
sample: Seasons with >= 120 legal balls; bowlers with >= 6 such seasons (n = 52).
finding: R Ashwin beat the league in 14 of 14 seasons (mean -0.83 runs/over). 7 bowler(s) beat the league in every qualifying season. The median bowler beat the league in 55% of seasons.

title: Bowling under different match conditions
sample: League: all regulation balls. Paired test: bowlers with >= 500 legal balls in each innings (n = 68). Venues: 15 with >= 20 full matches.
finding: Bowling second, the median qualifying bowler's economy is 7.86 vs 8.05 bowling first (Wilcoxon p = 0.009, a statistically significant but small difference); second-innings totals are partly truncated by successful chases, which may contribute. Death-over wicket rates are similar in both innings (13.4 vs 13.6 balls per wicket). At high-scoring venues economy is 8.46 vs 8.00 at low-scoring venues, with boundary % 18.4% vs 16.3% and balls per wicket 21.1 vs 21.5.

title: Chasing success by first-innings score
finding: Chases of sub-140 totals succeed 83% of the time, falling to 51% for 160-179 and 18% for 200+ (n = 143). Chase success falls in every successive band. In 2023-24, targets of 180-199 were chased 45% of the time (n = 29, CI 28-62%) - the 'safe' total has moved upward with the scoring increase, though 2023-24 samples are small.

title: Chasing success by required run rate and wickets in hand
sample: 1047 full non-D/L chases; 1037 still live after over 10. Cells with < 10 chases are omitted.
finding: After 10 overs, needing 8-10 an over with 8-10 wickets in hand the chase is won 67% (n=206); with only 5-7 wickets in hand it falls to 42% (n=108). Needing 10-12 with 8-10 wickets: 42% (n=90). Both required rate and wickets in hand matter (rank correlation of required rate with winning at over 10: rho = -0.59). These are observed frequencies from real match states, not a modelled 'pressure index'.

title: Scoring with different numbers of wickets remaining
sample: 250,618 legal balls in cells with >= 1,000 balls.
finding: Within the same phase, losing wickets slows scoring: in the middle overs the run rate is 8.40 with 0-1 wickets down vs 6.14 with 6+ down; in the death overs 11.35 vs 8.82. Comparing within a phase matters - overall, death overs have both the most wickets down and the highest scoring, which would hide this effect.

title: Successful vs unsuccessful chase patterns
finding: Successful chases are ahead from the start: Powerplay median run rate 8.33 vs 7.50, losing 1.09 vs 1.93 wickets on average (Mann-Whitney p = 1.5e-11 for run rate, 4.8e-33 for wickets). The biggest wicket gap is in the middle overs (1.72 vs 3.10). Caution: winning chases often end early, so their death-overs sample is smaller and selected (n = 504 vs 472).

title: Close-match performance by team
sample: 391 close matches; teams with >= 20 close matches (n = 10).
finding: Gujarat Titans have the best close-match record (69.6% of 23, CI 49-84%) and Deccan Chargers the worst (37.9%). But only 0 team(s) have an interval excluding 50%, and the chi-square test does not reject 'all teams equal' (p = 0.13). Close-match and other-match win % correlate at rho = 0.30 (p = 0.40). The data does not support a 'clutch team' effect beyond what chance explains.

title: Batting and bowling in narrow-margin matches
sample: 391 close matches. Batters with >= 150 balls in close matches and >= 500 in others (n = 91).
finding: Run rate in close vs other matches by phase: Powerplay 7.85 vs 7.86; Middle 7.75 vs 7.81; Death 10.35 vs 9.70 - close matches score faster at the death, where narrow finishes are decided. For batters, median strike rate in close matches is 133.2 vs 131.0 otherwise (Wilcoxon p = 0.640). Individual 'big-match' differences such as DJ Hussey (+29.4) come from 150-400 balls and are within normal sampling noise.

title: Final-overs scoring in successful vs unsuccessful chases
finding: Chases that were eventually won needed a median 7.40 per over from over 16, vs 13.60 for those lost: the gap in match position before the final five overs is already large. In the final overs, winning chases scored at 11.51 per over on average vs 8.59 for losing chases; losing chases also lost 0.64 wickets per over vs 0.28 for winning chases. Winning chases often finish before over 20, so later overs include fewer winning matches.

title: Team scoring by phase (vs league)
finding: Best phase-adjusted batting: Powerplay - Kochi Tuskers Kerala (+0.89); Middle - Punjab Kings (+0.18); Death - Royal Challengers Bengaluru (+0.59 runs/over). Run shares are similar across teams (Powerplay 28-36% of runs), so differences are in efficiency rather than structure.

title: Team wicket-taking by phase (vs league)
finding: Most wicket-taking relative to the league: Powerplay - Gujarat Titans (+0.65 per 120 balls); Middle - Rising Pune Supergiants (+0.34 per 120 balls); Death - Gujarat Titans (+0.88 per 120 balls). The spread is about +/-2.4 wickets per 120 balls.

title: Batting and bowling strength vs league
finding: Chennai Super Kings have the best net rating (+0.28 runs/over: batting +0.11, bowling -0.16). Net rating tracks win % closely (rho = 0.75, p = 0.001, n = 15; established franchises only: rho = 0.90, n = 8) - run-rate differential is a sound summary of team quality.

title: Season-adjusted performance and consistency across seasons
finding: Chennai Super Kings are the most consistent (season win % SD 11.0, above 50% in 12 of 15 seasons); Delhi Capitals the least (SD 15.0). Binomial chance alone, with ~15 matches a season, would produce an SD of about 13 points. Observed SDs (11-15) exceed this for 4 of 8 franchises, so most season-to-season swings in win % are of the size chance alone produces; the season-level record is a noisy guide to underlying strength.

title: What separates winning and losing performances (first innings)
finding: Winning first innings outscore losing ones in every phase; the gap is largest in the Death overs (median 10.80 vs 9.40 per over). Winners lose fewer middle-overs wickets (2.01 vs 2.41) and hit more boundaries at the death (23.9% vs 18.3% of balls). Mann-Whitney p-values for run rate: Powerplay 2.2e-12, Middle 6.0e-26, Death 1.7e-20.

title: Scoring patterns: early vs recent IPL
finding: From 2008-12 to 2023-24 the Powerplay run rate rose from 7.43 to 9.08 and sixes per over from 0.18 to 0.33; death-overs sixes per over rose from 0.41 to 0.63. Dot-ball % fell in 2 of 3 phases (Powerplay 49.6% -> 43.0%). Balls per dismissal changed little (Powerplay 24.5 -> 23.7; death 11.7 -> 12.1): the extra runs came without wickets becoming rarer, consistent with more aggressive batting.

title: Venue scoring patterns by phase
finding: Brabourne Stadium is the highest-scoring venue relative to the league (Powerplay +0.92, Middle +0.39, Death +0.32 runs/over) and MCA (Pune) the lowest. Venues above the league in all three phases: Brabourne Stadium, M Chinnaswamy Stadium, Eden Gardens. 10 of 15 venues are on the same side of the league in all three phases, and Powerplay and death-over venue effects correlate at rho = 0.42: venue character is partly consistent across phases, but 5 venues switch between above and below the league depending on the phase.

title: Batting-first vs chasing outcomes across venues (test)
finding: Chase win % ranges from 43.4% to 64.9% across venues, but the chi-square test gives chi2 = 11.9 (dof = 14), p = 0.61: the data does NOT provide significant evidence that venue changes the batting-first/chasing balance. The league-wide chasing edge (~54%) is the safer planning assumption than venue-specific rates.

title: Do high-scoring venues have different bowling patterns?
finding: Across venues, higher scoring goes with more boundaries (rho = 0.69, p = 0.004) and fewer dot balls (rho = -0.27, p = 0.328), while wicket-taking relative to expectation is only weakly related (rho = -0.05, p = 0.850). Of these, only the boundary relationship is statistically significant: high-scoring grounds are mainly 'boundary grounds' rather than 'no-wicket grounds'.

title: First-innings score vs match outcome ('par score')
finding: The par score was 170 in 2008-22 (95% CI 166-174) and 183 in 2023-24 (CI 171-196). Around par, each extra 10 runs adds about 9 percentage points of win probability (2008-22). The estimated rise in par is +13 runs (bootstrap 95% CI +1 to +26); the interval excludes zero, so the par score has risen beyond what sampling noise explains.

title: Is a predictive model justified?
sample: Train 14,950 over-end states from 832 chases; test 3,864 states from 215 chases.
finding: Pre-match prediction is not justified: the only pre-match signals in the data (toss 50.8%, chasing ~54%, venue - E2 not significant) are near coin-flip, squads change every season and there is no player availability data, so any model would be weak and misleading. The in-chase task IS supported: on unseen 2022-24 seasons the logistic model reaches AUC 0.880 and Brier 0.144 vs 0.254 for the base rate and 0.154 for the lookup table (best: Logistic regression (4 features)). Coefficients have the expected signs (required rate -0.43, wickets in hand +0.56). It is a transparent win-probability curve suitable for a dashboard visual - not a betting or selection tool.
